name: Suggestibility
description: Memory can be altered by suggestion, leading questions, or misleading post-event information. The person's later recollection may incorporate the suggestion as if it were part of the original experience.
design_relevance_note: Relevant mostly to research operations and trust-sensitive systems: interview wording, survey prompts, AI summaries, support scripts, and corrective messaging can accidentally plant details instead of neutrally recovering what a user actually experienced.
prevalence_note: Common in eyewitness, survey-method, and misinformation research, and occasionally important in trust-and-safety or research-ops practice, but not a standard named interaction-design law.

findings.description: Reported to show that eyewitness memory can incorporate misleading post-event information, and that accurate source monitoring (correctly attributing where a specific memory detail actually came from) plays a protective role against this suggestibility. Independently confirms and mechanistically extends the corpus's existing misinformation-effect evidence (Loftus 2005) with a specific cognitive mechanism (source monitoring) that Loftus's own review doesn't isolate. This description is drawn from this entry's own prior review note and well-established secondary characterization, not independently verified against the primary text this session.
findings.source_title: The eyewitness suggestibility effect and memory for source

findings.description: Reviewing three decades of misinformation-effect research, Loftus concluded that misleading post-event information can impair memory for the original event and that warnings reduce this suggestibility only under limited circumstances.
findings.source_title: Planting misinformation in the human mind: a 30-year investigation of the malleability of memory.
